title: What is Helm, and how do Helm charts and chart versioning help you template, parameterize (`values.yaml`), install, upgrade, and roll back Kubernetes application releases across environments?
shortTitle: Helm Charts, Versioning, and Templating Releases Across Environments

s1_definition.profdef: Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A Helm chart is a versioned bundle of templated Kubernetes manifests plus a default `values.yaml`. Templates use Go templating to substitute values, so one chart can render different manifests per environment by supplying a different values file. `helm install` creates a named release, `helm upgrade` applies changes and records a new revision, and `helm rollback` reverts to a previous revision. Charts carry two versions: the chart `version` (the package itself) and the `appVersion` (the application image it deploys).
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, imagine the blueprint for setting up a new branch: the counters, the vault, the signage. Writing that blueprint by hand for every city is error-prone. Helm is a reusable branch blueprint where the city-specific details — branch size, number of counters, local manager name — are filled in from a small settings sheet. Dev gets a two-counter branch, production gets a fifty-counter branch, from the same blueprint. If a new branch setup goes wrong, Helm lets you revert to the previous working layout in one command.
s1_definition.oneliner: Helm packages Kubernetes manifests into versioned charts, parameterizes them with values files per environment, and manages install, upgrade, and rollback as tracked release revisions.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes. A Helm chart is a versioned bundle of templated Kubernetes manifests plus a default `values.yaml`. Templates use Go templating to substitute values, so one chart can render different manifests per environment by supplying a different values file. `helm install` creates a named release, `helm upgrade` applies changes and records a new revision, and `helm rollback` reverts to a previous revision. Charts carry two versions: the chart `version` (the package itself) and the `appVersion` (the application image it deploys).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, imagine the blueprint for setting up a new branch: the counters, the vault, the signage. Writing that blueprint by hand for every city is error-prone. Helm is a reusable branch blueprint where the city-specific details — branch size, number of counters, local manager name — are filled in from a small settings sheet. Dev gets a two-counter branch, production gets a fifty-counter branch, from the same blueprint. If a new branch setup goes wrong, Helm lets you revert to the previous working layout in one command.

**One line to remember:** Helm packages Kubernetes manifests into versioned charts, parameterizes them with values files per environment, and manages install, upgrade, and rollback as tracked release revisions.

sections.s2_technical:
A chart is a directory with a `Chart.yaml` describing its name and versions, a `templates/` folder of manifest templates, and a `values.yaml` with defaults. Templates reference values with expressions like `{{ .Values.replicaCount }}` and can use helpers, conditionals, loops, and named templates in `_helpers.tpl`. This is how one chart produces a Deployment with two replicas in dev and ten in production — the manifest is identical, only the injected values differ.

Parameterization per environment is the core benefit. You keep a base `values.yaml` and layer environment overrides such as `values-dev.yaml`, `values-staging.yaml`, and `values-prod.yaml`. At deploy time you select the right overlay: `helm upgrade --install transfer ./chart -f values-prod.yaml`. Production might set a larger resource request, a production database host, and `minReplicas: 10`, while dev sets small values and a dev host, all from the same chart.

Versioning is two-dimensional and matters for governance. The chart `version` in `Chart.yaml` follows semantic versioning and changes when the chart's templates or defaults change. The `appVersion` tracks the application image version the chart deploys. Keeping them distinct lets you ship a chart fix (say, adding a readiness probe) without bumping the app, or roll out a new app image without touching chart structure. Charts are published to a chart repository (an OCI registry or a classic Helm repo) and consumed by version, which gives reproducible, auditable deployments.

The lifecycle commands map to release revisions. `helm install transfer ./chart` creates release `transfer` at revision 1 and stores the rendered manifests and values in a release secret. `helm upgrade transfer ./chart -f values-prod.yaml` renders again, diffs, applies, and records revision 2. `helm history transfer` lists all revisions with their chart version and status. `helm rollback transfer 1` reverts to revision 1 by re-applying its stored manifests, creating a new revision that is a copy of the old state. A senior nuance is that Helm rollback, like a Deployment rollback, reverts the Kubernetes objects Helm manages but does not undo external side effects such as a database migration run by a Helm hook, so I still design migrations to be backward compatible. Helm also supports lint, `--dry-run`, `template` for rendering without applying, and `--atomic` so a failed upgrade automatically rolls back, which I always enable for banking releases.
sections.s3_banking:
At the National Bank of India we deploy the Transfer Service to dev, staging, and production. Two real problems drove adopting Helm.

Problem 1 — we used to keep three near-identical copies of raw YAML, one per environment, and they drifted: a probe added in production was forgotten in staging, so a bug reached production that staging could not have caught. This is exactly what a single parameterized Helm chart fixes — one template, three small values files, no drift.

Problem 2 — a production upgrade shipped a bad configuration and we needed to revert fast under pressure. Hunting for the previous YAML by hand was slow and risky. This is exactly what Helm revisions and `helm rollback` fix — one command restores the last good release.

The mini-project is a runnable Java simulation of a `HelmEngine` that renders a templated Deployment from a base values map overlaid with an environment values map, maintains a release history of revisions, and supports install, upgrade, and rollback with an `--atomic` flag that auto-reverts a failed upgrade. We render the Transfer Service for dev and production, perform a bad upgrade, and roll back, logging each revision. The `Account` model carries Rajesh and Priya to tie it to the banking flow.

##### 4c. Chart files (templates and values)

```yaml
# Chart.yaml — two versions: chart package vs app image
apiVersion: v2
name: transfer-service
version: 1.4.0        # chart version (bump when templates/defaults change)
appVersion: "v7"      # application image version this chart deploys
```

```yaml
# values.yaml — defaults (dev-friendly)
replicaCount: 2
image: { repository: nbi/transfer-service, tag: v7 }
resources: { requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi" } }
dbHost: dev-db.internal
```

```yaml
# values-prod.yaml — production overrides only
replicaCount: 10
resources: { requests: { cpu: "1", memory: "1Gi" } }
dbHost: prod-db.internal
```

```yaml
# templates/deployment.yaml — one template, rendered per environment
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: {{ .Release.Name }}-transfer }
spec:
  replicas: {{ .Values.replicaCount }}
  template:
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: transfer
          image: "{{ .Values.image.repository }}:{{ .Values.image.tag }}"
          env:
            - name: DB_HOST
              value: {{ .Values.dbHost }}
          resources:
            requests:
              cpu: {{ .Values.resources.requests.cpu }}
              memory: {{ .Values.resources.requests.memory }}
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile and run the Helm simulation
javac -d out sim/src/main/java/com/bank/helm/*.java
java -cp out com.bank.helm.HelmDemo

# Real Helm usage across environments
helm lint ./transfer-chart
helm upgrade --install transfer-dev  ./transfer-chart                         # dev defaults
helm upgrade --install transfer-prod ./transfer-chart -f values-prod.yaml --atomic
helm history transfer-prod            # list revisions with chart version + status
helm rollback transfer-prod 1         # revert to revision 1
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a Transfer chart at version 1.4.0, deployed to dev and production, then a bad production upgrade.

Step 1 — The chart defines base values of 2 replicas, image v7, and a dev database host. The HelmEngine holds these as the base values map.

Step 2 — Installing to dev uses no overrides, so the rendered Deployment has 2 replicas pointing at the dev database. This is release `transfer-dev` revision 1.

Step 3 — Installing to production overlays `replicaCount=10` and the production database host onto the base. The rendered Deployment has 10 replicas pointing at the production database, from the exact same template. This is release `transfer-prod` revision 1. A transfer of fifty thousand rupees from Rajesh to Priya runs on the production release.

Step 4 — A production upgrade ships a bad image v8 and fails its health check. Because the upgrade used `--atomic`, Helm does not leave the release in a failed state; it automatically rolls back to the last good revision, which re-applies revision 1's manifest with image v7.

Step 5 — The release history shows revision 1 deployed, and the atomic rollback recorded as a new revision that is a copy of the good state, so production is healthy on v7 again with no manual YAML hunting.

Final output:

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  transfer-chart (version 1.4.0, appVersion v7)
    ├── values.yaml (replicaCount=2, dev-db)
    └── templates/deployment.yaml
            │

   │ render with values                        │
   ▼                                           ▼
  dev overlay (defaults)              prod overlay (-f values-prod.yaml)
  replicas=2, dev-db                  replicas=10, prod-db
   │                                           │

  transfer-dev rev1                    transfer-prod rev1 (deployed)

```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
            LLD — HelmEngine (render + revisions)
  ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Template Method: render() fills a fixed manifest shape        │
  │ Memento: Release stores a revision for rollback               │
  │ Command: install/upgrade/rollback are tracked operations      │
  │ Decorator (values): env overlay decorates base values         │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Release=state, HelmEngine=lifecycle (separate jobs)        │
  │ O: new env = new values map, no engine change                 │
  │ L: any Release revision is interchangeable for rollback        │
  │ I: engine exposes install/upgrade/rollback only               │
  │ D: demo depends on HelmEngine API, not render internals       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌───────────────────────────┐ owns  ┌────────────────────────┐
  │ HelmEngine                │◆─────▶│ Release                │
  │ - chartVersion:String     │  *    │ - revision:int          │
  │ - baseValues:Map          │       │ - chartVersion:String   │
  │ - history:List<Release>   │       │ - values:Map            │
  │ + install/upgrade/rollback│       │ - status:String         │
  └───────────────────────────┘       └────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a release ──────────────────────────────────
  [install rev1] ──upgrade ok──→ [rev2 deployed] ──rollback──→ [rev3=copy]
        │                              │
        └── upgrade fail(--atomic) ────┘ auto-revert to last good

  ── Call Chain (prod bad upgrade) ─────────────────────────────
  1. helm.install("transfer-prod", prodValues) → rev1
  2. helm.upgrade(... v8-bad, healthy=false, atomic=true)
  3.   → health FAIL → rollback("transfer-prod", 1)
  4.   → new rev2 = copy of rev1 (v7) deployed
  5. helm.printHistory() → audit trail
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Helm is the package manager for Kubernetes, and it solves the problem of managing raw manifests by hand across many environments. A Helm chart is a versioned bundle of templated manifests plus a default values file. The templates use Go templating to substitute values, so a single chart can render a two-replica Deployment pointing at a dev database or a ten-replica Deployment pointing at a production database, purely by supplying a different values file. That eliminates the configuration drift that happens when you maintain separate copies of YAML per environment.

Parameterization works through layered values. I keep base defaults in the chart's values file and layer environment-specific overrides such as a production values file that bumps replicas, resource requests, and the database host. At deploy time I select the overlay with a flag, so dev, staging, and production all come from the same template with no divergence in structure, only in the injected values.

Versioning is deliberately two-dimensional. The chart version tracks the package itself and changes when templates or defaults change, while the app version tracks the application image the chart deploys. Keeping them separate means I can ship a chart fix, like adding a readiness probe, without pretending the application changed, and I can roll out a new application image without altering chart structure. Charts are published to a repository and consumed by version, which makes every deployment reproducible and auditable.

The lifecycle commands map to tracked revisions, and that is what makes Helm powerful operationally. Install creates a named release at revision one, upgrade applies changes and records a new revision, the history command lists every revision with its chart version and status, and rollback reverts to a chosen revision in a single command. In my banking project at the National Bank of India I always deploy production with the atomic flag, so a failed upgrade automatically rolls back to the last good release instead of leaving production half-broken. That turned a tense, manual YAML hunt during an incident into a one-command recovery, while a single parameterized chart ensured dev, staging, and production never drifted apart again.
